clue.text: Sam knew Joe vaguely in Simon piece

indicators.note: done vaguely, the three names lose their shape and their letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Two men named Sam and Joe have only a hazy acquaintance with someone called Simon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vaguely' rearranges SAM KNEW JOE. 'Simon' looks like a person both men half know, but it is the American playwright Neil Simon, whose comedy has this title.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil Simon wrote the 1992 stage comedy of this title, so it is a play by him.

clue.text: Chronicler of Rievaulx I confused with Adler

indicators.note: being confused, the letter and the surname are jumbled into a different order

explanation.surface: Someone mistakes a medieval monk-historian for the psychologist Alfred Adler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confused' rearranges I and ADLER. Rievaulx is a Cistercian abbey in Yorkshire whose twelfth-century abbot wrote histories and lives of kings.
explanation.definitionFit: Aelred, also spelt this way, was abbot of Rievaulx and wrote historical works such as a genealogy of English kings.

clue.text: Church reader like Richardson?

explanation.surface: A man reads the lesson in church, much as the novelist Samuel Richardson might have done.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Richardson wrote his novels Pamela and Clarissa entirely as letters, so the question mark marks him as a writer of epistles in a secular sense.
explanation.definitionFit: In church the person who reads out the New Testament letter is so called; a writer of letters, as Richardson's novels in letters made him, has the same name.

clue.text: Wide prediction of Beckett's verse

parts.note: W is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a wide, a ball bowled out of the batsman's reach
an astrological forecast of someone's fortunes is a prediction

explanation.surface: Someone is struck by how broad a forecast Samuel Beckett's poetry makes.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Beckett's first separately published work was a 1930 poem about Descartes with this punning title.
explanation.definitionFit: Beckett's prize-winning early poem bears this title, so it is a piece of his verse.

clue.text: Thin French model is renowned detective

parts.note: maigre is the French word for thin
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so 'model' can give T

explanation.surface: A skinny French fashion model turns out to be a famous sleuth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' suggests a catwalk; the T comes from Ford's Model T.
explanation.definitionFit: Georges Simenon's Paris police inspector is one of fiction's best-known sleuths.

clue.text: Villain heard in body of church

indicators.note: heard tells us the word for villain is only to be spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a knave is a dishonest rogue or villain

explanation.surface: A scoundrel is caught in the middle of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: KNAVE has a silent K, so said aloud it matches the church word.
explanation.definitionFit: The central part of a church, where the congregation sits, is its main body.

clue.text: A blonde I deceived in the library

indicators.note: deceived letters are misled out of their places, so A BLONDE I is rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tricked a fair-haired woman inside a library.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deceived' rearranges A BLONDE I. 'The library' is a fair definition because the Oxford University library is known simply as 'the Bod'.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford University's great research collection, founded by Thomas Bodley, is the archetypal university library.

clue.text: "Good are invariably ungrammatical" (Wilde)

parts.note: a quotation with a gap after 'Good': fill it with the noun that also names Wilde's 1891 volume of critical essays

explanation.walkthrough: Wilde's line runs 'Good ___ are invariably ungrammatical', and the missing word is also the title of his book of essays including 'The Decay of Lying'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde published a collection of four critical essays under this title, and the word completes his aphorism about good aims.

clue.text: Substantive epithet for publicity on returning peacemakers

parts.note: an ad is a piece of publicity

indicators.note: returning means the little word on is turned back to front

parts.note: UN, the United Nations, sends out peacekeeping forces

explanation.surface: An epithet describing a publicity campaign for returning peace envoys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning' turns 'on' round. 'Substantive epithet' is a grammar term: an adjective used as a noun, as in 'the rich'.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammarians use the term for an adjective standing as a noun, an epithet acting as a substantive.

clue.text: Italian composer is very pale, going to Northern Ireland

parts.note: an albino lacks skin pigment and is very pale

explanation.surface: An Italian composer, pale as a ghost, travels to Belfast.
explanation.definitionFit: Tomaso Albinoni was a Venetian Baroque composer, famous for an Adagio attributed to him.

clue.text: One of his works remains

parts.note: read 'Remains' as a title: a writer whose collected pieces were published posthumously as 'The Remains' of their author

explanation.walkthrough: 'Remains' looks like a verb about surviving writings, but it is the title of the Elizabethan poet Fulke Greville's posthumous collection (1670).
explanation.definitionFit: The Elizabethan poet Fulke Greville's verse treatises appeared after his death in a book called The Remains, so it is a work of his.

clue.text: Image said to be not working

indicators.note: said asks for the word for not working to be pronounced, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: someone idle is not working

explanation.surface: A picture is reported to be broken.
explanation.definitionFit: An image or statue worshipped as a god is a graven image.

clue.text: A prodigy he misled, writing in symbols

indicators.note: misled letters go astray from their order, so A PRODIGY HE is rearranged

explanation.surface: A child genius was led astray by him, using a code of symbols.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misled' rearranges A PRODIGY HE.
explanation.definitionFit: Representing ideas by pictorial characters, as in Chinese script, is writing with symbols rather than letters.

clue.text: Chef is sent in error for change of setting

indicators.note: in error means the letters are put down wrongly, so CHEF IS SENT is reshuffled

explanation.surface: A cook is dispatched by mistake to a new location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In error' rearranges CHEF IS SENT.
explanation.definitionFit: In the theatre, moving the scenery between scenes changes the setting of the play.

clue.text: Noble flowers from Queen Elizabeth's brother

parts.note: an earl is a nobleman
a river is a flower in the crossword sense: something that flows

explanation.surface: A nobleman arranges flowers sent from the Queen's brother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowers' reads as blooms but means things that flow. The Queen is Elizabeth Woodville, wife of Edward IV, not Elizabeth I.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Woodville, second Earl Rivers, was the brother of Edward IV's queen, Elizabeth Woodville.

clue.text: American sage featured in A Room with a View

definitions.text: featured in A Room with a View

explanation.surface: An American wise man appears in E.M. Forster's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Forster's novel has a father and son of this name, George and old Mr Emerson.
explanation.definitionFit: Ralph Waldo Emerson was the sage of Concord, and Forster's novel has a free-thinking father and son with the same surname.

clue.text: Keynes was concerned with these consequences of peace

definitions.text: Keynes was concerned with these consequences of peace

parts.words: Keynes was concerned with these consequences of peace
parts.note: points to Keynes's 1919 book on the Versailles treaty: the missing adjective completes its title, '___ Consequences of the Peace'

explanation.walkthrough: Keynes's attack on the Versailles settlement was titled 'The ___ Consequences of the Peace'.
explanation.definitionFit: Keynes's 1919 book on the treaty of Versailles dealt with the financial effects of the peace settlement.

clue.text: Lady Nicholson inspired him, or her

definitions.text: Lady Nicholson inspired him, or her

parts.words: Lady Nicholson inspired him, or her
parts.note: Lady Nicolson is Vita Sackville-West, wife of Harold Nicolson, the model for Virginia Woolf's hero who changes sex mid-novel

explanation.walkthrough: 'Him, or her' fits because Woolf's title character lives for centuries and wakes up a woman halfway through.
explanation.definitionFit: Vita Sackville-West, married to Harold Nicolson, inspired Woolf's 1928 novel whose hero becomes a heroine.

clue.text: Seat of amateur reviewer?

parts.note: a piece of furniture that gives its name to the stay-at-home critic who judges without expertise

explanation.walkthrough: An amateur pundit is called an '___ critic', after the comfortable chair they sit in.
explanation.definitionFit: The upholstered chair gives its name to the idiom for someone who comments without experience, an armchair critic.

clue.text: Grade female connected by Joyce with aviation pioneer, say

definitions.text: connected by Joyce with aviation pioneer, say

parts.note: a step is a grade or degree on a scale
a hen is a female bird

explanation.surface: A woman of some rank is linked by James Joyce with an early flier.
explanation.walkthrough: Joyce's hero Stephen Dedalus takes his surname from Daedalus, who flew on wings of wax and feathers, hence 'aviation pioneer, say'.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce named his hero Stephen Dedalus, joining the first name to the mythical inventor who first flew.

clue.text: Lear knew him well enough, and his name

definitions.text: Lear knew him well enough, and his name

parts.words: Lear knew him well enough, and his name
parts.note: echoes King Lear's words to the blinded earl, 'I know thee well enough; thy name is ...'

explanation.walkthrough: In King Lear IV.vi the mad king recognises his blinded old courtier with 'I know thee well enough; thy name is ___'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Earl of this title is the blinded nobleman whom Lear names in the heath scene.

clue.text: Deity spoils planet

explanation.definitionFit: The Roman god of war, a verb meaning damages, and the fourth planet from the sun all share this word.

clue.text: Habitat of Barham's bird

parts.note: Richard Barham's Ingoldsby Legends include the poem about a thieving jackdaw living in a French cathedral city

explanation.walkthrough: Barham's 'The Jackdaw of ___' tells of a bird that steals a cardinal's ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Barham's jackdaw lived at the French cathedral city, so it is the bird's home.

clue.text: … elves for fear / Creep into —s and hide them there " (A Midsummer Night's Dream)

definitions.text: elves for fear / Creep into —s and hide them there " (A Midsummer Night's Dream)

parts.words: elves for fear / Creep into —s and hide them there " (A Midsummer Night's Dream)
parts.note: Puck's speech about Oberon and Titania's quarrel: the gap is the tiny oak-fruit holder that frightened fairies hide in

explanation.walkthrough: Puck says the fairies quarrel so that 'all their elves for fear / Creep into acorn-cups and hide them there'.
explanation.definitionFit: The cup-shaped base that holds an oak's nut is small enough for Shakespeare's fairies to hide in.

clue.text: Practical animals like Gus and Macavity

definitions.text: Practical animals like Gus and Macavity

parts.words: Practical animals like Gus and Macavity
parts.note: T.S. Eliot's Old Possum's Book of Practical ___ includes Gus the Theatre one and Macavity the Mystery one

explanation.walkthrough: Gus and Macavity are pets in T.S. Eliot's Old Possum's book of verse, later the source of a musical.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's poems about Gus and Macavity describe household felines.

clue.text: Superior little room, say, in Egyptian shorthand style

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase for the superior little room is to be spoken, giving a word that sounds alike

parts.note: superior means higher, and a little room under the roof is an attic

explanation.surface: A better small room is found in an ancient Egyptian writing style.
explanation.walkthrough: Said quickly, 'higher attic' sounds like the term for the cursive script Egyptian priests used.
explanation.definitionFit: Egyptian priests used a simplified cursive form of hieroglyphs, an abbreviated writing system.

clue.text: e.e.cummings's father moved through depths of it

definitions.text: e.e.cummings's father moved through depths of it

parts.words: e.e.cummings's father moved through depths of it
parts.note: quotes the cummings poem 'my father moved through dooms of love', whose first stanza ends 'my father moved through depths of ___'

explanation.walkthrough: Cummings's paradox 'depths of ___' pairs opposites, like 'sames of am' elsewhere in the poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Cummings's line sets depth against its opposite, the dimension of tallness or elevation.

clue.text: Emphasis on air for soprano, perhaps

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece written on another follows it, so the emphasis comes after the tune

parts.note: an air is a song or tune
stress is emphasis

explanation.surface: A singer puts emphasis on the melody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' warns that a soprano is only one example of a female singer; the definition is by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A soprano is an example of a female singer.
